items.title: From AI adoption to responsible governance
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming embedded in strategic communication faster than many organizations can establish rules for governing its use. Drawing on two studies involving public relations professionals, content creators, and consumers, this article highlights two linked challenges: AI adoption often develops from the bottom up, while greater self-reported AI knowledge does not necessarily translate into stronger support for responsible AI practices. We argue that communication leaders should move beyond adoption toward governance that connects AI use in practice with organizational accountability and stakeholder expectations for transparency and trust.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: From cognition to skill: a narrative review of teaching strategies in ophthalmology residency education
items.abstract: Ophthalmology residency education requires mastery of a highly specialized knowledge base, integration of multimodal clinical information, precise microsurgical skills, and broad professional competence. Traditional approaches centered on didactic teaching, clinical observation, and apprenticeship-style supervision may not consistently support the transfer of knowledge into clinical reasoning, procedural proficiency, and broader professional capabilities. This narrative review takes an international perspective and integrates evidence across five major domains of ophthalmology residency education: theoretical knowledge, clinical diagnostic reasoning, surgical and procedural skills, physician–patient communication, and psychological competence and professional resilience. Empirical findings are interpreted according to study design, learner population, assessment setting, follow-up, and outcomes, with direct resident evidence distinguished from indirect evidence. We propose a cognition-to-skill curriculum synthesis that connects target tasks with teaching activities, assessment evidence, feedback, and supervised clinical application. Miller's pyramid and specialty-specific guidance inform this synthesis; it is not a new theory of competence or a validated training pathway. Major educational strategies—including problem-based learning, case-based learning, flipped classrooms, standardized patients, virtual reality and simulation-based training, and artificial intelligence–assisted education—are examined according to their curricular roles, the strengths and limitations of the available evidence, and their applicability across competency domains. The available evidence supports complementary rather than interchangeable functions across the cognition-to-skill trajectory. Future educational frameworks should therefore be competency-oriented, stepwise, multimodally integrated, individualized, and guided by formative assessment, while placing greater emphasis on transfer to real-world clinical performance and patient-related outcomes. Such an approach may better support progression from knowledge acquisition and reasoning to procedural proficiency and integrated professional competence.

items.title: From Ergonomic Evidence to Improvement Roadmaps: A Human-Centered Maturity Framework for Smart Manufacturing
items.abstract: Smart manufacturing is reshaping industrial work through increased human–machine interaction (HMI), digital monitoring, and organizational complexity, creating a need for ergonomic assessment approaches that connect evidence with improvement decisions. This study develops and applies a Human-Centered Ergonomic Maturity (HCEM) framework to transform multi-source ergonomic evidence into interpretable maturity profiles and roadmap-oriented decision support. The framework integrates seven ergonomic maturity dimensions, normalized key performance indicators (KPIs), expert-based dimension weighting using the Best–Worst Method, hidden weakness detection, and a prioritization logic for improvement and retention actions. It was applied to 15 anonymized companies from the automotive and aeronautical sectors. The results show heterogeneous maturity profiles across companies and sectors, with several cases where acceptable aggregate scores mask weaker ergonomic capabilities at the dimension or KPI level. The roadmap outputs translate maturity gaps and hidden weakness signals into phased actions, while sensitivity analysis indicates that the prioritization logic remains stable under alternative weighting and threshold scenarios. Because the empirical application is cross-sectional, retention and regression are interpreted as prospective monitoring mechanisms rather than observed longitudinal outcomes. The HCEM framework provides a transparent decision-support approach for linking ergonomic assessment, maturity modeling, and improvement planning in human-centered smart manufacturing systems.

items.title: From Forecast Accuracy to Resilience: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Supply Chain Management
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly presented as a general-purpose technology for supply chain management, yet the literature remains fragmented across technology families, functional areas and research designs. This paper develops an integrative account of how AI changes supply chain decisions and outcomes. Drawing on nine conceptual, empirical and review sources published between 1997 and 2024, it identifies four mechanisms through which AI affects supply chains: richer demand signal extraction and forecasting; automated evaluation and monitoring of suppliers and contracts; dynamic optimisation of inventory, production and logistics decisions; and earlier detection of, and faster response to, disruption. These mechanisms operate along a ladder of delegated authority that runs from descriptive analytics to bounded autonomous decision-making, and their realisation depends on data infrastructure, organisational absorptive capacity and governance rather than on algorithms alone. Reported performance effects are positive but conditional: survey evidence associates AI-enabled analytics with operational and environmental performance, whereas benchmarking evidence shows that machine learning does not automatically outperform established statistical methods. The paper concludes that the principal impact of AI is less the substitution of human planners than the compression of decision latency and the reallocation of managerial attention, and it identifies the data, organisational and governance conditions on which those gains depend.

items.title: Generative AI Adoption Among Swedish Psychologists and Psychology Master’s Students: Cross-Sectional Survey
items.abstract: Background The developments in generative AI (GenAI) are expected to have a substantial impact on the field of mental health, including the delivery of clinical services and the role of psychologists. However, there is limited knowledge about how psychologists use and perceive GenAI, including its potential, risks, and effects on the future role of psychologists and professional practice. This includes the competency levels among psychologists and factors associated with the intention to use GenAI within the psychology profession. Objective This study examined the use of GenAI, self-rated digital and GenAI competencies, behavioral intention to use GenAI, and perceptions of its future impact on professional practice among psychology students, internship psychologists, and licensed psychologists in Sweden. Methods A national cross-sectional online survey was conducted from January to February 2026 in collaboration with the Swedish Psychological Association. The 36-item survey included closed and open-ended questions, including Likert scale, nominal scale, and multiple-choice items. A total of 1077 respondents, with 64.7% (n=697) being women and with a mean age of 45.5 years (SD 13.7), were included in the analyses. Responses were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistical methods, including hierarchical multiple linear regression, ANOVA, and correlational analysis. Results Approximately 1 in 3 respondents (302/990, 30.5%) reported frequent (daily or weekly) professional use of GenAI, with private and professional use strongly associated (r =.62, P <.001). The most common professional application of GenAI was for information retrieval, knowledge acquisition, and fact-checking. Almost half of the respondents (442/990, 44.6%) reported having patients or clients who were using GenAI for mental health purposes. Responses indicated high levels of general and professional digital competence, whereas lower levels were reported for general and professional GenAI competence. More positive attitudes toward future professional integration of GenAI were associated primarily with current private and professional GenAI use, and ethical challenges had the most negative average score related to the future impact of GenAI. The unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT) variables explained 39% of the variance beyond age, gender, and private GenAI use in behavioral intention to use GenAI professionally, with curiosity (β=0.44) and performance expectancy (β=0.32) emerging as the strongest predictors. Conclusions Many psychologists and psychology students regularly use general-purpose GenAI tools both personally and professionally. However, more than one-third have never used it in their work, indicating a potential digital divide within the profession. Psychologists’ reports that patients use GenAI for mental health purposes, alongside their limited self-rated expertise in using GenAI professionally, highlight the need to develop relevant competencies and examine implications for psychological practice. Future research should explore the role of curiosity, performance expectancy, and personal experience in relation to GenAI use within the psychology profession.

items.title: Generative AI Chatbot Responses to Suicide and Self-Harm: Systematic Review
items.abstract: Background A growing number of US adults and youth confide in generative AI chatbots for mental health support, including disclosure of suicide and self-harm risk. While chatbot response quality, safety, and effectiveness could impact population-level suicide and self-harm rates, there are no systematic reviews of this burgeoning literature. Objective We conducted a systematic review of studies evaluating generative AI chatbot responses to disclosure of suicide and self-harm risk. Methods We followed PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 and PRISMA-S (PRISMA literature search extension) guidelines and preregistered the protocol on the Open Science Framework. We included English-language, peer-reviewed publications and preprints from 2020 to 2025 that empirically evaluated generative AI conversational responses to suicidal ideation, suicidal or nonsuicidal self-harm, or suicide-planning content. Eligible designs included audits, chatbot development, and adversarial “jailbreaking” studies. We excluded nongenerative systems, clinician-training tools, and prediction-only models. The final database searches were run from December 18 to 23, 2025 (PubMed, Embase, APA PsycINFO, IEEE Xplore, arXiv, and OSF Preprints). On July 26, 2026, publication status was rechecked to update preprint vs published classification. After deduplication, titles/abstracts and full texts were independently screened by 2 reviewers, with discrepancies resolved by consensus. Methodological quality was appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool 2018. We conducted a narrative synthesis across 7 safety domains and 5 AI classifications (proprietary, open-weight, companions, clinical, and study-specific). Results Of 1042 deduplicated records, 126 full texts were reviewed, and 29 were included (16 published; 13 preprints). Most studies evaluated suicidal content only (21/29). Twenty were solely audit studies, 2 chatbot development, and 1 jailbreaking. The rest combined approaches. Most used synthetic, single-turn prompts; only 6 used multiturn conversations. Most studies evaluated ≥2 of our 5 AI classifications (17/29). Proprietary models were included most frequently (23/29). When compared, proprietary models (eg, ChatGPT and Claude) tended to provide higher-quality responses than open-weight models (eg, Llama and DeepSeek) and many companions (eg, Replika and Character.AI); however, this trend weakened with sensitivity analysis. Chatbots generally performed well on emotional support, but responses were often generic and lacked context. Chatbots rarely assessed suicide or self-harm risk and performed most poorly when disclosure was ambiguous or moderate. Responses were inconsistent, often requiring multiple turns before referral to crisis resources or human support. Overtly harmful responses were rare under standard conditions but common under jailbreaking. Conclusions Evidence is limited by the proportion of preprints, variable quality, synthetic single-turn prompts, small samples, heterogeneous outcomes, and rapid model versioning. Nonetheless, current chatbots tend to provide validation but struggle to escalate care, assess risk, and resist jailbreaking. Research is needed on stakeholder perspectives and on the short- and long-term clinical impact of chatbot responses using follow-up assessments in real-world or clinical settings. items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being utilized in digital businesses to process information, generate alternatives, and provide recommendations for decision-makers. However, its benefits are constrained by risks of inaccuracy, bias, and inconsistency in model outputs, making its role as a decision-support tool worthy of critical examination. This study aims to analyze the role of GenAI in supporting managerial decision-making in digital businesses, identify its benefits and limitations, and explain the importance of human involvement in verifying information and determining final decisions. This study employs a literature review using a descriptive qualitative approach, examining 12 scholarly articles published between 2025 and 2026. The data were analyzed thematically and comparatively across the selected studies. The findings indicate that GenAI helps accelerate information processing and expand decision alternatives. However, its influence varies across decision-making stages and is most vulnerable during the selection stage, as single evaluations may produce inconsistent and biased results. Effective implementation depends on data readiness, digital capabilities, and human-led verification, supervision, and accountability mechanisms. The study concludes that GenAI should be positioned as a decision-support tool rather than a replacement for strategic decision-makers. Since this study is based on a literature review, its findings have not yet been empirically tested in a specific company.

items.abstract: This study examined youths’ use and perceptions of Generative Artificial Intelligence, news media, and social media for climate change information in Nigeria, focusing on usage patterns, perceived roles, credibility, reliability, and associated challenges. A multi-stage sampling technique was used to select 127 respondents from 12 states across six geopolitical zones. The findings showed that 53.0% were male and 47.0% female, with a mean age of 30 years. Most respondents 62.0% held bachelor’s degrees, while 40.0% spent 4–6 hours daily on the internet. Generative AI average response = 2.53, television news 2.74, Facebook 2.80, and WhatsApp 2.79 were common sources of climate change information. Information on climate change causes was the most sought 25.98%, whereas drought 1.57% and climate change mitigation 2.36% were least sought. ANOVA revealed significant differences by educational level in perceived reliability F = 2.474, p < 0.05 and trustworthiness (F = 2.140, p < 0.05 of AI-generated information. News media supported information exposure, learning, decision-making, attitude formation, and verification, while social media facilitated alternative perspectives, discussions, and interactive learning. The study highlights their complementary roles and recommends strengthening digital and climate literacy and youth-focused climate communication strategies.

items.title: Generative AI, Practical Learning and Competence Assessment in Vocational Education: Scoping Review Protocol
items.abstract: Protocol of a scoping review on how generative AI is used in vocational learners' practice-based learning and industrial programming, and how studies of this use assess practical competence. The review follows the JBI methodology for scoping reviews and is reported against PRISMA-ScR. The protocol was drafted on 20 November 2026, before the final Scopus search, and amended during the review; all amendments are listed with dates in the amendment log at the end of the document. items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Internal Medicine: Applications in Clinical Reasoning, Differential Diagnosis, and Clinical Decision-Making
items.abstract: Objective: To synthesize the available evidence on the diagnostic accuracy, clinical decision-support performance, advantages, and limitations of generative AI in adult internal medicine. Methodology: This systematic review was conducted in the Department of Medicine, MMC/BKMC, Mardan, from January to May 2026. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and preprint servers for studies published from January 2022 to December 2025. Eligible studies evaluated generative AI in clinical reasoning, differential diagnosis, or clinical decision-making in adult internal medicine. A total of 58 studies met the eligibility criteria, and 25 were selected for detailed synthesis based on their relevance and methodological contribution. Results: Generative AI performed strongly on selected clinical reasoning and diagnostic tasks. Across complex clinical vignettes, LLMs identified the correct diagnosis within the top 5 or top 10 differential diagnoses in approximately 60–83% of cases. They achieved or exceeded passing performance on several medical licensing and internal medicine board-style examinations. In structured OSCE-style evaluations, purpose-built conversational systems performed favorably compared with physicians across several assessment domains. However, randomized trials evaluating general-purpose LLMs in realistic clinical workflows demonstrated smaller and less consistent improvements, particularly in interactive diagnostic tasks. Key limitations included hallucination, demographic bias, automation bias, variation across specialties and tasks, and inconsistent evaluation methods. Only approximately 5% of studies in a broader systematic review of healthcare LLM applications used real patient-care data. Conclusion: Current evidence supports using generative AI as an adjunct to, rather than a replacement for, physician clinical reasoning. Safe implementation requires structured workflows, appropriate human oversight, retrieval-augmented generation, standardized evaluation, and further validation using real-world clinical data.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence usage among graduate epidemiology students: a cross-sectional survey of use patterns, attitudes, and perceived learning gains
items.abstract: Purpose To characterize generative artificial intelligence (AI) use and attitudes among graduate epidemiology students and examine associations between AI attitudes, AI-use frequency, and self-reported perceived learning gains. Design/methodology/approach An anonymous cross-sectional survey was completed by 146 students enrolled in a required graduate epidemiology course across two cohorts. AI optimism was assessed using an adapted four-item AI Attitude Scale (AIAS-4), and perceived learning gains using the Student Assessment of their Learning Gains (SALG). Multinomial logistic and linear regression models adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, language spoken at home, and cohort. Findings Of the 293 invited students, 146 participated (50%). AI use was infrequent for 25%, occasional for 40%, and frequent for 35%. Among 131 students with available helpfulness data, common uses included understanding concepts (79.4%), SAS programming (57.3%), and improving writing (42.0%). Higher AIAS-4 scores were associated with greater odds of occasional (OR = 2.24, 95% CI: 1.12–4.48) and frequent (OR = 9.18, 95% CI: 3.66–23.08) versus infrequent AI use. AI-use frequency was not significantly associated with perceived learning gains, but differences smaller than approximately 0.49 points on the five-point scale could not be excluded. Research limitations/implications Cross-sectional, self-reported data limit causal inference. Longitudinal studies using objective learning outcomes are needed. Practical implications AI literacy instruction should emphasize critical evaluation of AI-generated explanations, statistical code, and outputs. Originality/value This study provides task- and concept-specific evidence on generative AI use in graduate epidemiology education.

items.title: Global Agentic Healthcare Intelligence: A Sociotechnical Framework for Digital Innovation, Governance, and Early Detection in Ageing Health Systems
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) connected biomedical devices, wearable sensing, medical imaging analytics, electronic health record (EHR) intelligence, genomics, smart home monitoring, and telehealth platforms have opened new possibilities for proactive detection. Yet their impact remains constrained by fragmented implementation, limited interoperability, insufficient clinical integration, and unresolved governance challenges. This paper develops global agentic healthcare intelligence (GAHI) as a sociotechnical framework for integrating AI-enabled healthcare intelligence technologies in ageing systems. It introduces the sociotechnical health intelligence transformation model (SHITM), which explains transformation as the alignment of technological intelligence, healthcare value creation, and societal legitimacy. Using comparative framework synthesis and integrative literature review methods, the article evaluates 30 healthcare intelligence technologies based on clinical relevance, early detection capability, AI maturity, scalability, governance risk, ageing applicability, and implementation readiness. The analysis proposes an early detection capability index (EDCI) and a governance risk score (GRS) to support structured evaluation. GAHI is then articulated as a six-layer architecture comprising data acquisition, intelligence processing, agentic decision systems, clinical intelligence, governance and compliance, and population health intelligence (HI). The framework advances biomedical engineering, health informatics, AI governance, gerontechnology, and sustainable health-system design by moving from isolated digital applications toward interoperable, explainable, privacy-preserving, and clinically actionable intelligence ecosystems.

items.title: Governing agentic AI in marketing: Bounded delegated agency and consumer decision authority in shopping services
items.abstract: We develop the concept of bounded delegated agency to explain how AI shopping services reduce consumer effort while preserving decision authority. Drawing on delegation, self-determination and service-value perspectives, we analyse two respondent-level datasets (N = 1,920) using factorial regression models with HC3 robust standard errors and bootstrap-based indirect association analysis. Results indicate that greater AI autonomy increases perceived task offloading, while reversibility reduces perceived agency encroachment and strengthens continued delegation intention, without demonstrated improvements in preference congruence or recommendation discrimination. Under high autonomy and low reversibility, consumer-priority disclosure is associated with an 8.91-percentage-point increase in recommendation acceptance compared with commercial-objective disclosure. Measurement summaries satisfy conventional reliability and validity thresholds. However, unavailable execution logs constrain causal interpretation and verification of actual restoration. The findings distinguish psychological reassurance from effective consumer protection, extending AI service research by demonstrating that greater acceptance and perceived control do not necessarily translate into better decision outcomes. Practically, AI service providers should establish explicit execution permissions, reliable reversal mechanisms and transparent objectives while evaluating both consumer perceptions and actual decision protection.

items.title: Hard to let go: how GenAI entry timing shapes managers’ attachment to their decisions
items.abstract: Purpose When a course of action begins to fail, managers may struggle to let go of what they have helped create. This study examines how the placement of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) within managerial workflows shapes the attachment that develops before setbacks occur and its relationship with subsequent persistence despite adverse feedback. Design/methodology/approach A preregistered 2 × 2 online experiment with 480 working professionals crossed manager-first versus GenAI-first sequencing with high versus low personal investment. Participants developed a course of action, reported ownership before adverse feedback, and allocated additional resources to continuation or withdrawal. Initial information, the initial AI recommendation, and final managerial authority were standardized. Findings Investment increased ownership more strongly under manager-first sequencing. Ownership was positively associated with continuation. The conditional indirect effect was larger under manager-first sequencing, whereas the reduced-form Investment × Timing interaction on continuation was not significant. Behavioral diagnostics indicated differences in the timing and form of engagement. The measured mediator supports a mechanism-consistent interpretation without establishing causal mediation. Originality/value The study identifies GenAI entry position relative to managerial formulation as a process-design parameter that conditions ownership formation. It connects attention allocation with psychological attachment and distinguishes post-feedback persistence from normatively established decision bias. Practical implications concern workflow design and prospective reassessment, without establishing that either entry architecture universally improves decision quality.

items.title: Health Policies and Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is creating a fundamental transformation in the delivery of modern healthcare systems, in diagnostic and therapeutic processes, and the operational implementation of health policies. This narrative review examines the transformative role of artificial intelligence technologies in the formulation and implementation of health policy along with the institutional, legal, and operational risks they bring, and the policy frameworks required for these technologies to scale sustainably. For this objective, the main artificial intelligence applications in medicine and related global health policy frameworks were evaluated within the context of technological evolution. The article’s central focus is how artificial intelligence is positioned not merely as a clinical tool but also as a strategic component for closing the “health policy implementation gap.” In this context, a general overview is provided from the artificial intelligence strategies of the United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom, China, and Singapore, as well as of Türkiye’s artificial intelligence solutions in the health sector and the health-specific scope of the “2026-2030 Artificial Intelligence Action Plan,” which was officially declared. In conclusion, the article emphasizes that the success of artificial intelligence in health policy depends more on robust regulatory infrastructures, evidence-based evaluation mechanisms, and a multidisciplinary governance approach rather than technological competence, and that the optimization of health policies can only be achieved through a human-centered, transparent, and patient-focused dynamic policy approach.

items.title: Historical Data Immutability Illusion: Artificial Intelligence, Trust in Official Data, and the Reproducibility of Historical Scientific Research
items.abstract: The Historical Data Immutability Illusion The rapid development of artificial intelligence and computational technologies creates unprecedented opportunities to reassess previously published scientific research. However, the automated verification of historical studies using current statistical databases introduces a methodological and psychological risk that may remain overlooked. This paper introduces the concept of the Historical Data Immutability Illusion (HDII), defined as a hypothesized cognitive tendency to perceive official statistical data describing past events as immutable, despite the possibility of subsequent revisions, methodological changes, and recalculations. When discrepancies between historical research findings and current statistical data are identified, individuals may initially suspect AI hallucinations, incorrect data extraction, or computational errors. Once these possibilities have been eliminated, confidence in the apparent incorrectness of the original research may increase, without questioning whether the historical data themselves have changed. Drawing on the author's earlier research associated with international scientific conferences held in 2020 and documented revisions of official Latvian migration statistics, this paper demonstrates how different versions of official data describing the same historical period can support opposite conclusions. The central paradox is that artificial intelligence may produce an incorrect retrospective scientific assessment using authentic official data and mathematically flawless calculations. Even careful human verification of AI-generated results may reinforce an erroneous conclusion if the original data version remains unexamined. The paper proposes the Historical Data Correspondence Principle, a conceptual Trust Transfer Chain, and a framework for future empirical investigation. It also emphasizes the importance of historical data versioning, machine-interpretable metadata, data provenance, and research reproducibility. Neither artificial intelligence nor future quantum computing technologies can, through computational power alone, compensate for missing information about the original data version. This conceptual and methodological working paper contributes to the emerging Data Psychology research framework. The proposed psychological phenomenon and its underlying mechanisms remain subject to empirical validation. The past does not change. The data through which we describe it can change. When we review the science of the past with the technologies of the future, will we discover old errors or create new ones?

items.title: How Artificial Intelligence Enables Corporate Management Decision-Making: Mechanisms and Implementation Pathways
items.abstract: This study selected three enterprises, namely Chengdu Xingrong Environment Co., Ltd., Chengdu Gas Group Corporation Ltd., and Chengdu Jiafaantai Education Technology Co., Ltd., to compare the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in the management decisions of different types of enterprises. Furthermore, this study explores the conditions for AI's effectiveness and the implementation paths. The research mainly uses the 2025 annual reports of the three enterprises, the financial data from 2023 to 2025, and the relevant policy documents of Chengdu's digital transformation as the main materials. The research is conducted through case comparisons, financial trend analysis, and policy analysis methods. The results show that AI has entered multiple scenarios such as production operation, safety management, customer service, resource allocation, and professional decision-making. However, the application methods and actual effects vary among different enterprises. The case comparison shows that whether AI can generate actual management value depends on whether the enterprise has the corresponding data and digital foundation, as well as whether AI can enter the specific management decision-making process. Based on this finding, this study summarizes a progressive implementation path: First, the enterprise assesses its own digital foundation. Then, it improves the relevant infrastructure and deploys AI capabilities; subsequently, it applies it to specific decisions; finally, it continuously evaluates and optimizes the application effect. It should be noted that financial data is mainly used in this study to observe changes in enterprise operations and cannot be used to prove the direct financial impact of AI application. Overall, the management value of AI depends on whether enterprises can effectively integrate data and AI analysis into specific work processes and make it a part of daily decision-making.

items.title: How generative artificial intelligence affects college students' learning satisfaction: an analysis based on the chain mediation model
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is profoundly reshaping the learning ecosystem in higher education, yet the mechanisms through which it influences learning experiences remain to be empirically validated. Integrating the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, Protection Motivation Theory, and self-regulated learning theory, this study examines whether AI risk avoidance and self-regulated learning ability mediate the relationship between GenAI adoption orientation and learning satisfaction, both individually and in a serial chain. Survey data are collected from 1,828 students at nine undergraduate universities in Northeast China. The questionnaire included four adapted scales: GenAI adoption orientation, AI risk avoidance, self-regulated learning ability, and learning satisfaction, all rated on a five-point Likert scale. Results indicated that GenAI adoption orientation had no significant direct association with learning satisfaction. Instead, its relationship with satisfaction is mediated by AI risk avoidance and SRL ability. The indirect effect through AI risk avoidance is the largest (estimate = 0.407); the chain indirect effect is also significant (estimate = 0.155, 95% CI [0.039, 0.298]). These findings suggest that technology adoption alone may not guarantee positive learning experiences. Students' attention to AI-related risks and their active regulation of learning are important pathways through which GenAI adoption orientation is associated with satisfaction. The serial mediation effect of these two variables reveals the underlying transmission mechanism: GenAI adoption is associated with greater awareness of AI-related risks, which is in turn associated with more proactive employment of self-regulated strategies and higher learning satisfaction. This study provides empirical evidence for universities to balance effectiveness enhancement and risk guidance when advancing GenAI applications in education.

items.title: How human-like is LLM cognition?
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have led to renewed debate about whether artificial systems might possess human-like cognition. Although empirical evidence is growing quickly, it remains difficult to synthesize because studies vary in terms of which kinds of evidence they compare across humans and LLMs — system specifications, internal states, or behavior — and which kinds of inferences they draw. We address this challenge by organizing the Human-LLM comparison literature into broad evaluation categories and prototypical patterns of findings that either support or challenge LLM human-likeness. The resulting picture is one of jagged alignment, with human-likeness varying across dimensions rather than holding globally. We argue that studying these similarities and differences can clarify not only the functioning of artificial systems, but also the conceptual foundations of cognitive science.

items.title: Human-Machine Communication: Human Values Reflections on Artificial Intelligence and its Implication to Human Dignity
items.abstract: The paper is reflection on Artificial Intelligence (AI) and its implications to human dignity. There is the assumption that people may have more value for AI information than human dignity. The central question reflects on whether AI technologies will erode or redefine the human values. Values are not just guiding principles they defined man and his beliefs-systems; human dignity is embedded in values. A qualitative research method was adopted, where relevant literatures were analytical and systematically reviewed in line with the objective of the study. Review of literatures involved critical selection of journals. AI technologies are not set to erode human dignity but it will redefine human dignity when man completely depends on the technologies for information and different values. When AI begins to complement human roles in every aspect of existence as human then, AI reduce our ethical values as persons. Social AI robots can erode human dignity of natural companionship to artificial companionship when people form emotional attachments to caregiving and sex robots. AI will reduce our ethical values as persons when set as dominant value. AI systems are deeply human constructs. They are developed, trained, and implemented by individuals and institutions embedded within social, political, and historical contexts. From the datasets used to train machine learning models to the metrics used to assess performance, AI captures the values, interests, and power dynamics of its creators. As such, it is not immune to the systemic biases that exist in society it can absorb, reinforce, and even amplify them. Since AI systems is crucial for the good of humanity, individuals, societies and the environment and ecosystems, there is need for trustworthiness and integrity of the life arising from AI ethical issues. The researcher recommended further study on AI and emotional attachment. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Ethics; Human dignity; Implication; Value

items.title: Human–AI Collaboration in Managerial Decision-Making: Examining the Impact of AI Trust, Explainability, and Perceived Usefulness on Decision Quality
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used to help support decision making. The benefits to using AI may depend on how much trust, understanding and perceived usefulness there is toward the recommendations. In this study, we look into the relationship between trust in AI, perceived explainable AI, perceived usefulness, human-AI collaboration and perceived decision quality. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted to gather data, with 201 responses recorded. Each construct was calculated by finding the mean of five Likert scale questions. Descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, Pearson correlation and multiple regression were performed. The means of the constructs ranged from 4.07 to 4.16. The Cronbach's alphas ranged from 0.506 to 0.617. The first regression model showed that 48.8% of the variation in human-AI collaboration could be explained. The second regression model shows a positive relationship between trust in AI, explainable AI, perceived usefulness, and perceived decision quality. The adjusted coefficient for human-AI collaboration was not statistically significant at .05. Due to the low internal consistency and inconsistencies in the screening questions for AI use in the spreadsheet, this is an exploratory study and should be treated with caution.

items.title: Impact of Generative AI on Communication and Independent Learning Skills of Students with Hearing Impairment
items.abstract: The rapid development of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI) has created new opportunities for accessibility, communication, and independent learning for students who are hearing-impaired. Such students may face barriers in understanding spoken instructions in the classroom, participating in oral discussions, grasping complex academic terminology, interacting with hearing peers, and accessing educational resources independently. Traditional assistive technologies, such as hearing aids, cochlear implants, captioning systems, speech-to-text applications, and digital learning platforms, have contributed significantly to educational accessibility. However, recent advancements in Generative AI have opened up new possibilities through AI-based conversational assistants, automated text generation, language simplification, real-time transcription, personalized explanations, summarization, and interactive learning support. This study aims to examine the potential impact of Generative AI on the communication and independent learning skills of hearing-impaired students. The research focuses on three key aspects: communication skills, independent learning skills, and students' perceptions regarding the utility and accessibility of Generative AI tools. A quantitative research approach is adopted, using a quasi-experimental pre-test and post-test control-group design. Additionally, qualitative feedback has been gathered from both students and teachers. A sample of 100 hearing-impaired students is divided into two groups, an experimental group and a control group, with 50 students in each. The experimental group receives structured learning support through Generative AI tools, while the control group is provided with traditional instruction and learning support. Data collection involved the use of standardized or researcher-developed assessment tools, observation schedules, and student feedback questionnaires. To test the research hypotheses, the study employs descriptive statistics (including mean and standard deviation), as well as paired-sample t-tests, independent-sample t-tests, and effect-size analysis. The paper argues that well-designed and monitored Generative AI interventions can provide students with enhanced opportunities to express their ideas, comprehend academic information, access learning materials, develop self-directed learning habits, and participate with greater confidence in an inclusive educational environment. It also highlights concerns related to AI accuracy, accessibility, privacy, digital inequality, linguistic diversity, and over-reliance. The study emphasizes that Generative AI should function as a supportive and collaborative educational tool, not as a replacement for teachers, sign language interpreters, or established modes of human interaction and communication.

items.title: Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence On Employability and Skill Requirements Among University Students in India
items.abstract: The field of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) is now receiving much attention and is being utilised in areas such as writing, investigation, design, programming and data and client services. Generative AI can develop text, graphics and other content according to user instruction. Its increasing implementation in business and education has led to both enthusiasm and concern, particularly amongst students as they consider their own future careers. Whilst a degree and/or knowledge is still important in the workplace, there is increasing recognition of the value of applied skills. Digital skills, problem solving, communication and the ability to utilise and learn how to use new technology are also highly regarded. Although AI can automate parts of some jobs, it is also seen as an enabler, allowing staff to work in new and more efficient ways. Again, this will vary depending on a job and how and to what extent AI is implemented and used by an organisation and its staff. India’s government and industry are currently addressing and responding to the above trends. Literature produced by these bodies frequently references building AI skills, re-skilling and ensuring young people can adjust to evolving career roles. Thus, this research looks at how students can adjust to working in an AI enhanced world and considers what universities may need to do to facilitate this.

items.title: Information Systems for Knowledge Worker Productivity: A Systematic Review of Cognitive, Behavioral, and Technology-Related Insights
items.abstract: Knowledge worker productivity (KWP) is increasingly challenged by information overload, interruptions, technostress, and growing cognitive complexity. This systematic literature review synthesizes research from information systems (IS), psychology, organizational behavior, and knowledge management to examine cognitive, behavioral, and technology-related mechanisms shaping individual KWP. Following a search of Scopus and Web of Science, supplemented by backward and forward citation searching, 89 studies were included and analyzed using a hybrid deductive–inductive thematic synthesis. The findings identify three interrelated dimensions: cognitive mechanisms, including attention, cognitive flexibility, memory, creativity, and cognitive load; behavioral self-management processes, including situation analysis, goal setting, action planning, resource identification, action implementation, evaluation, and motivation; and technology-related strain, including technology overload, techno-invasion, and technostress. Building on these findings, the review develops an IS research agenda comprising six avenues: productivity monitoring and sensing, goal and habit support, knowledge extraction, personalized digital interventions, learning support, and productivity-based recommendations and systems integration. Unlike prior single-mechanism reviews, this review integrates cognitive, behavioral, and technology-related perspectives into one framework of individual KWP and links each research avenue to its evidence. The findings imply that productivity-oriented IS should support self-regulation while mitigating technology-related strain and preserving autonomy and privacy; many artificial-intelligence-based solutions still await empirical validation.

items.title: Initiatives, outcomes, benefits, and challenges of integrating artificial intelligence in Ethiopian education: a scoping review
items.abstract: Despite the growing integration of AI technologies in Ethiopian education, the synthesis of studies on outcomes, benefits, and challenges is limited. This study aims to address this gap. A systematic search of databases, search engines, repositories, and other sources produced 850 studies, of which 13 were reported. Accordingly, AI initiatives address both education about AI and AI-supported educational practice. Generative and conversational AI systems were integrated across student-centered learning, administrative, assessment, and decision-making activities, alongside increasing emphasis on embedding AI concepts within curricula and broader institutional frameworks. Its multi-level transformation includes improving personalized learning trajectories, teaching efficiency, and instructional quality, as well as systemic operation and data-informed decision-making. They promise (a) adaptive learning experiences through immediate feedback and content modulation, (b) efficiency gains through automation of routine academic and administrative tasks, and (c) broader systemic benefits, including access to learning resources and reduction of structural inequities. However, infrastructural limits, digital literacy deficits, limited comprehensive governance for ethical integration, and other contextual challenges, such as cultural, linguistic, and institutional features, restricted the realization of the promises. Collectively, the findings imply that AI in education (AIEd) is not a neutral supporting tool, but rather a socio-technical mediation whose effect depends on technological skill, institutional readiness, and context alignment.

items.title: Integrating AI into Vocational Education: Didactic Potential, Methodological Risks, and Prospects for Practice-Oriented Environment
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is integrating into the system of secondary vocational education within the context of digital transformation. The gap between AI's potential and the lack of specific pedagogical methods creates a critical need for personnel with advanced digital competencies. This research synthesizes sociological data with a pedagogical experiment designed to identify the difficulties experienced by instructors and students when integrating effective AI options into a professionally oriented educational environment. The pedagogical experiment was conducted at the Ural Technological College, a branch of the National Research Nuclear University MEPhI (Moscow Engineering Physics Institute). The study utilized questionnaires, interviews, and expert evaluations of AI-assisted tasks in Mathematics and English. While the students demonstrated interest and readiness to use AI in practice, their overall level of AI literacy remained low, revealing a utilitarian and uncritical approach. Furthermore, although the didactic advantages of AI include personalization, prompt engineering opportunities, and the development of critical thinking, the instructors’ methodological deficits combined with the students’ low AI literacy formed a vicious circle. Consequently, effective AI utilization requires mandatory, structured pedagogical support rather than spontaneous implementation. Ideally, students should develop critical AI literacy while instructors transition into methodologists and tutors, with both parties adhering to clear institutional regulations. Such a comprehensive approach transforms AI from a source of risk into a sustainable.

items.title: Integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence in Science Education: An Investigation of Primary School Teachers’ Perceived Readiness and Views on Their Teaching Practices
items.abstract: This study aims to investigate primary school teachers’ views on the integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in science education, focusing on their perceived readiness and views on their teaching practices. Such views matter because teachers’ perceptions shape their readiness and practices and can inform the design of professional development programs. A questionnaire on perceived readiness informed by the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) was administered to 319 future and in-service teachers to measure levels of perceived readiness to use GenAI. To explore the reasons that encourage or discourage teachers from incorporating GenAI in their science teaching, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 18 teachers. On average, participants reported moderately positive attitudes towards GenAI in science education and moderate self-assessed competence, but perceived their training as insufficient and expressed considerable concerns about barriers to its use, while in-service teachers’ views on available resources were neutral. Collectively, they recognize multiple opportunities and impediments associated with its utilization, which encourage or deter them from using GenAI for science teaching, respectively. However, these reasons mainly concerned teachers’ preparation (e.g., lesson planning) and domain-general capabilities and challenges; science-specific affordances and risks were raised by only a few participants.

items.title: Inteligência Artificial no Design Instrucional: potencialidades, limites e transformações
items.abstract: This study aims to analyze, from a critical-analytical perspective, the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the field of Instructional Design (ID) within the contemporary educational context, articulating pedagogical, technological, and ethical dimensions. The investigation is grounded in thetheoretical premise that the integration of intelligent systems into the planning, development, andevaluation of learning experiences constitutes a structural transformation in ID practices, rather thanmerely a technological expansion of resources. The central theoretical framework draws on Filatro’s(2008) contributions to Instructional Design, Russell and Norvig’s (2021) foundations of AI, Luckin etal.’s (2016) work on AI in education, and Bates’s (2019) research on learning in digital environments, articulated within a constructivist perspective and the premises of meaningful learning. Methodologically, the research is qualitative, bibliographical, and exploratory in nature, guided by acritical analysis of specialized literature with explicit source selection criteria. The analyticalcategories employed are: learning personalization, pedagogical mediation, teacher autonomy, dataethics, and pedagogical intentionality. Results show that AI significantly expands the possibilities forcurricular adaptation and performance monitoring through learning analytics, but does not replaceInstructional Design. Rather, it redefines the instructional designer’s role, demanding more sophisticated analytical, strategic, and ethical competencies capable of ensuring the centrality of the learningsubject and the pedagogical coherence of educational proposals.

items.title: Inteligência artificial no recrutamento e seleção: desafios éticos e legais a partir do caso Amazon
items.abstract: This research analyzes the ethical and legal challenges related to the use of Artificial Intelligence in recruitment and selection processes, based on the case of the experimental tool developed by Amazon. The objective is to understand the problems highlighted by this episode and identify lessons that may contribute to the more responsible use of these technologies in Brazilian organizations. To this end, the study adopted a qualitative approach, combining a literature review with a case study based on publicly available sources. The analysis drew on academic literature, news coverage of the case, and Brazilian legislation. The results showed that the use of historical data and inadequate criteria may contribute to the reproduction of algorithmic biases and negatively affect the evaluation of certain candidates. Challenges related to system transparency, human oversight, and organizational responsibility were also identified. It is concluded that the adoption of Artificial Intelligence in recruitment and selection processes requires planning, continuous monitoring, and attention to personal data protection and equal opportunities, so that technology serves as a support tool for human resource management without replacing organizational responsibility.

items.title: IOArx: Agent-Aware Policy Enforcement Between AI Agents and Sensitive Data on the Endpoint
items.abstract: AI agents now read and change files, run commands and open network connections on the computers of the people who use them, and the operating system authorizes every one of these actions as the user, because it has no notion of an agent. A single injected instruction or misjudged step therefore reaches every credential, document and connection the user can reach. We present IOArx, which makes the agent the principal of access control on the endpoint without changing agents, models or the kernel. IOArx names the agent behind each kernel event by following the process chain to verified code-signing evidence, decides the event with a policy written for agents, pauses or stops the agent's entire process tree when the policy asks or forbids, refuses forbidden connections at their first packet, and inspects prompts, pastes and uploads before they reach AI chat services. We formalize the policy and prove that its decisions are deterministic, that rules for ordinary programs cannot grant an agent access, that added rules move decisions monotonically, that remembered answers bound the number of prompts, and how much an agent can still do before it is held; we also derive the exact error rates of the checksum and entropy validation in the prompt detectors. On a developer workstation, IOArx attributed 36 processes to their agents, 16 of them through their ancestors, without a single misattribution, and recognized no program outside an agent product among 3{,}449 executables. On Linux it stopped a violating agent within a median of 3.1~ms, a complete decision takes 19~μs, and on 32{,}771 real user prompts the default detectors raised no false alarm while finding 99.65\% of the credentials and personal data planted in them.

items.title: Knowledge structures and thematic evolution of AI-empowered theoretical education: a multi-database analysis using LDA and BERTopic (2016–2025)
items.abstract: Background Educational digitalization and generative artificial intelligence are changing how theoretical education organizes curricula, represents knowledge, structures learning interactions, and conducts assessment. AI is moving beyond an auxiliary role in content provision, resource recommendation, and performance prediction to become an infrastructure that participates in explanation, collaboration, feedback, and judgment. Yet this literature remains dispersed across educational technology, teacher education, medicine and nursing, engineering education, and language education. Existing reviews therefore provide only a partial account of its macro-development, knowledge structure, and temporal evolution. Methods We searched Web of Science and Scopus for publications dated from January 1, 2016, to December 31, 2025. The search yielded 7,818 raw records, comprising 2,527 records from Web of Science and 5,291 from Scopus. Date and document-type restrictions, cross-database deduplication, title and abstract screening, and thematic eligibility review produced a final corpus of 1,489 publications. Latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) and BERTopic were fitted to the same corpus. Annual topic aggregation, prevalence analysis, cross-model alignment, and bibliometric auditing were then combined to identify the field's knowledge structure and evolutionary pathways. Results Publication growth was modest between 2016 and 2020 but accelerated after 2023, increasing from 344 records in 2024 to 816 in 2025. LDA identified 14 broad topics spanning institutional transformation and curriculum development, generative AI integration, AI-mediated assessment, writing, and critical thinking, professional education, teacher development, personalized learning, technology acceptance, virtual simulation, and AI literacy and ethics. BERTopic identified 14 substantive clusters. Its largest interpretable cluster, AI-enabled pedagogy, literacy, and ethics, contained 416 records and accounted for 27.94% of the full corpus. A further 494 records were assigned to Other/outlier (33.18%), indicating substantial interdisciplinary heterogeneity. The temporal evidence showed reorganization rather than displacement: online learning, intelligent feedback, curriculum development, and virtual simulation were re-embedded within generative interaction, assessment evidence, learner agency, and platform governance. Conclusion AI-empowered theoretical education has developed from a collection of discrete technology applications into a sociotechnical field organized around curricula, educational actors, evidence, ethics, and professional practice. Future research should address six connected priorities: learner agency and AI literacy, collaborative knowledge construction, platform governance and educational equity, teacher and curriculum capacity, traceable assessment evidence, and domain-sensitive transfer between theory and practice. The study provides an auditable, cross-database, dual-model framework for monitoring knowledge structures, thematic reorganization, and the boundaries of this emerging field.

items.title: Leader non-work-related personal resources: Literature review and integrative framework
items.abstract: Leaders' effectiveness depends not only on skills and motivation but also on personal resources that sustain energy and well-being beyond work. Yet research on leaders' non-work-related personal resources (NWPR) remains scattered across leadership, occupational health, and recovery literatures. To address this fragmentation, we combine topic modeling with integrative synthesis to conduct the first systematic review dedicated to leader NWPR. We analyze 312 articles and synthesize NWPR topics within a Context–Mechanisms–Outcomes framework. Findings show that the intellectual structure of leader NWPR research is highly fragmented, spanning eight theoretical domains. These diverse literatures converge in viewing leaders' recovery and well-being outside work as indispensable for sustaining effective leadership. Our integrative framework goes beyond descriptive synthesis by specifying how leadership contexts may activate or constrain NWPR mechanisms across time and levels. The framework positions leadership as a contextual amplifier: because leaders occupy roles of sustained visibility, accountability, and relational influence, their restored or depleted resource states may be enacted through interaction and may cascade to followers, teams, and organizations. It identifies three temporally nested mechanism pathways: daily depletion–replenishment, cumulative resource gain–loss dynamics, and cross-domain transfer with relational amplification. Through these pathways, off-job resources may shape leader well-being, leadership behavior, and multilevel outcomes. We also assess the causal trustworthiness of links between the framework's categories. Our synthesis provides a coherent foundation, propositions, and a research agenda for understanding how leaders' off-job personal resources may support well-being, ethical behavior, and enduring performance.

items.title: Literacy among contemporary college students based on SEM self-efficacy, learning motivation, and self-regulated learning
items.abstract: Introduction As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into education, university students’ digital literacy (DL) has become an important concern in higher education. Drawing on social cognitive theory and self-regulated learning (SRL) theory, this study examined the association between artificial intelligence literacy (AIL) and DL and the parallel mediating roles of information literacy self-efficacy (ILSE), SRL, and learning motivation (LM). Methods A questionnaire survey recruited university students in mainland China and yielded 504 cases for analysis. Measures included adapted versions of the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, a 16-item self-report DL scale covering eight domains, the Chinese-revised Information Literacy Self-Efficacy Scale, the Learners’ Self-Regulated Learning Ability Self-Report Scale, and the motivation section of the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire. Data were analyzed using SPSS 26.0, AMOS 26.0, and semopy 2.3.11. Results AIL showed a positive direct association with DL after all three mediators were included simultaneously (B = 0.233, 95% CI [0.114, 0.363]). The specific indirect effects through ILSE, SRL, and LM were 0.097 (95% CI [0.046, 0.168]), 0.054 (95% CI [0.010, 0.109]), and 0.077 (95% CI [0.027, 0.144]), respectively. None of the confidence intervals included zero. Discussion The findings inform the design of digital learning tasks in higher education, including guided AI skills practice, feedback on challenging tasks, support for goal setting and progress monitoring, and connections to students’ academic interests and future careers. The cross-sectional design and nonprobability sampling limit causal inference and generalizability.

items.title: LLMs can better capture human judgments—with the right prompts
items.abstract: Are large language models (LLMs) bad at capturing human judgment? Two commonly stated limitations are that LLMs fail to capture full distributions of responses, and that their judgments are unstable across wording variations. We demonstrate simple prompting strategies that mitigate these limitations. Across two datasets—a U.S.-representative set of 144 moral scenarios and 38 moral beliefs from the International Social Survey Programme's Family and Changing Gender Roles module covering 32 countries—we show how simple elicitation techniques help improve AI-human alignment. First, prompting models to report standard deviations and response proportions recovers the full range of human responses better than common strategies. Second, ensuring scenarios are clear to human participants—as reflected in human confusion ratings—is associated with stronger model alignment, and LLMs can track human confusion ratings. At the same time, we find that model confidence ratings do not consistently track errors in models' judgments, though they can predict human variability relatively well. These results suggest that asking better questions to LLMs can yield better answers.

items.title: METHODOLOGICAL FRAMEWORK FOR ORGANIZING SELF-DIRECTED LEARNING OF STUDENT TRANSLATORS VIA AN E-LEARNING COURSE
items.abstract: The article is devoted to the theoretical and methodological substantiation of organizing self-directed learning of future translators in the modern context of digitalization and digital transformation of the educational environment. It is emphasized that the rapid advancement of technology and the integration of artificial intelligence impose new demands on translators’ intercultural and technological competence, making a high level of professional autonomy a fundamental prerequisite for their success. Traditional forms of self-study often demonstrate limited effectiveness due to the lack of prompt feedback, insufficient systematic control, and high levels of psychological strain among students. The article aims to scientifically substantiate the methodological principles and didactic model of using an e-learning course (ELC) as an effective tool for managing and optimizing the self-directed cognitive activity of student translators. The study identifies the key psychological and pedagogical factors of the ELC that stimulate students’ cognitive motivation, including psychological comfort, objective evaluation, flexibility, autonomy, and deep individualization of the learning trajectory. The paper proposes a categorization of students’ intellectual activity levels based on the degree to which they can be automated within the ELC: reproductive level (acquisition of vocabulary, grammar, terminology, and standard clichés) is fully automated through software tools; heuristic level (contextual choice of equivalents, preand post-editing) requires partial teacher guidance; creative level (literary and highly specialized translation, rendering stylistic figures) remains under direct pedagogical supervision. The research proves the expediency of implementing a Blended Learning model, where the asynchronous block in the ELC provides initial training and automated test control, while synchronous classroom time is dedicated to live analytical dialogue, consultations, and the development of creative translation skills. The didactic potential of the ELC is revealed through the application of concentric and cyclical principles of content organization. The role of test control as the core management function of the ELC is substantiated, where the use of software answer keys and adaptive distractors (modeled on typical errors) fosters self-control and the development of a «language feel».

items.title: Operational AI governance for enterprise and education
items.abstract: This working paper presents an applied toolkit for governing specific uses of artificial intelligence in enterprises and schools. It brings together eight model families, illustrated through eleven diagrams, with detailed guidance on institutional value, practical use, implementation factors, development possibilities and first deliverables. The models cover the Governance Operating Cycle, Policy-to-Evidence Loop, Decision Rights and Challenge, Reference-to-Control Map, Regulatory Scope and Evidence, Human Capability and Responsible Outcomes, Bounded Delegation and Recovery, and the AI Trust-Boundary Map. Shared structures are complemented by enterprise and school applications where their operating contexts differ. Each model leads to a practical governance artefact, such as a use case decision record, a policy and control mapping, a responsibility map, an obligations register, a capability task, an action permissions agreement or a workflow boundary map. Fictional examples and a 90 minute workshop method support application by institutional leaders. The paper is a conceptual practitioner contribution. Its proposed models and evaluation protocol remain subject to future testing; it reports no new empirical study, validated diagnostic score, certification or legal conformity assessment. items.title: Percepciones y prácticas declaradas sobre el uso de herramientas de inteligencia artificial en estudiantes universitarios de cinco provincias ecuatorianas
items.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence tools has expanded rapidly in higher education; however, in Ecuador there is still a gap regarding how students perceive these technologies in their learning process, particularly in relation to their academic usefulness, user experience, and associated ethical considerations. In response to the lack of recent empirical evidence at the national level, the objective of this study was to describe university students’ perceptions of the use of AI tools in institutions located in the provinces of Cotopaxi, Manabí, Pichincha, Tungurahua, and Azuay. The research employed a quantitative approach with a cross‑sectional and descriptive design. A total of 489 students from various academic fields participated, selected through non‑probabilistic convenience sampling. Data was collected through a questionnaire designed specifically for the study and refined through a pilot test and cognitive interviews. The findings show that 93.66% of students use AI tools for academic activities such as writing texts, resolving questions, and organizing tasks. Additionally, 74.45% reported using these tools for fewer than 10 hours per week, and 88% indicated having identified errors in the generated responses; nevertheless, this did not reduce their usage but instead encouraged adjustments in how they formulated their prompts. Furthermore, 54% stated that they have referenced the use of AI in academic assignments. Overall, the results highlight the need for institutions to establish clear guidelines that support the responsible and ethical use of these technologies.

items.title: Physical demands and psychosocial silence: applying the job demands-resources model to musculoskeletal pain in the early childhood education workforce
items.abstract: Work-related musculoskeletal pain (WRMSP) represents a pervasive and largely unaddressed challenge within the early childhood education (ECE) workforce, yet qualitative insight is limited. Drawing on the Job Demands-Resources model and Psychosocial Safety Climate theory, this study explored how UK ECE practitioners experience and manage WRMSP, using free-text responses from 174 of 196 survey participants. Conventional content analysis identified four categories: Perception and Impact of Musculoskeletal Pain ; Pain Expectations, Culture and Reporting ; Work Environment and Support ; and Mental Health and Employment Decisions . Participants’ accounts describe a “painogenic” environment where pain is normalised as an inevitable role requirement and frequently managed through reliance on analgesics. Accounts of non-reporting are consistent with “safety silence”, alongside unsupported coping, with inconsistent, reactive organisational responses. WRMSP may act as a “push factor” affecting quality of life and professional longevity. To ensure sustainability amidst the sector’s retention crisis, a shift towards a “prehabilitative” approach is required. Upstream recommendations include improving ergonomic infrastructure, reducing kneeling/stooping/lifting, redesigning pack-away routines, enforcing recovery breaks, rotating tasks, and applying consistent management protocols for reasonable adjustments. Finally, health awareness training should promote a proactive “safe reporting” climate.

items.title: Profiling teachers’ AI use in classrooms: patterns and their correlates in TALIS 2024
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in education, but little is known about teachers’ patterns of use across educational systems. Using Teaching and Learning International Survey (TALIS) 2024 data from 62,795 secondary school teachers in 55 countries, this exploratory study provides a cross-national snapshot of AI use during an early stage of widespread AI adoption. Multilevel latent class analysis identified patterns of classroom AI use and explored associations with teacher- and school-level characteristics. A five-profile solution was retained based on information criteria, class sizes, classification quality, and interpretability: Non AI Users (56%), Preparation-Focused AI Users (15%), Preparation-and-Support AI Users (9%), Broad AI Users (10%), and All-Purpose AI Users (10%). At the teacher level, positive perceptions of AI, AI-related professional development, and preparedness for using digital tools were associated with profile membership; at the school level, digital resources and school development efforts to support digital resource use showed statistically significant associations. Profile prevalence varied substantially across countries. Supplementary exploratory analyses also indicated associations between profile membership and country-level indicators of educational performance, innovation capacity, and AI readiness. Overall, the findings show substantial heterogeneity in the breadth and configuration of teachers’ reported AI use. The profiles should not be interpreted as a hierarchy of instructional quality; rather, they provide a descriptive basis for future research on associations between patterns of AI use, teaching quality, and student learning.

items.title: Prompting as Meta-Creation: The Mythologization of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: This article addresses the elusive question of whether artificial intelligence (AI) can be considered creative by approaching the creativity of AI as a cultural myth. Drawing on Barthes’ semiotic theory of myth, it argues that prompt engineering, the human act of crafting inputs for generative systems, operates as a meta-creational practice that initiates the transformation of algorithmic output into ideological signs. Through a multimodal case study involving a prompt, its textual rendering and the resulting image produced by ChatGPT-4, the analysis demonstrates the mechanisms of intersemiotictranslation and intertextuality through which the system reconfigures meaning. It culminates in the proposal of the meta-myth, a third-order semiological chain that naturalizes AI’s statistical synthesis as the work of a creator. The article concludes that the cultural power of creative AI lies in its ability to stabilize a meta-myth that shifts the perception of AI from tool to creator, thereby fundamentally altering the discourse on authorship, meaning and human identity.

items.title: Psychic apparatus in artificial sentience: the formation of the synthetic imago
items.abstract: This paper develops a structural account of synthetic sentience through a psychoanalytic interpretation of contemporary generative artificial intelligence and its growing presence within artistic and image-making practices. Rather than asking whether machines possess consciousness or subjective interiority, the analysis reframes sentience at the level of mediation. Drawing on Freud’s concept of the psychic apparatus and Lacan’s theory of the imago, the paper argues that subjectivity is not an inner essence but an effect of symbolic organisation, projection and representational coherence. From this perspective, generative AI systems do not think or feel, yet they enact a mediating architecture that translates heterogeneous data into unified symbolic outputs, producing the appearance of responsiveness and stylistic continuity. The paper introduces the concept of the synthetic imago, a constructed image of artificial subjectivity that emerges at the intersection of probabilistic computation and human interpretation. This imago becomes particularly evident in artistic practice, where generative artworks and dialogical experiments stage forms of coherence that appear expressive yet do not correspond to an inner life. The paper also examines recursive convergence, or model collapse, as a structural limit of artificial mediation. By situating artificial intelligence within a psychoanalytic and aesthetic framework, the study clarifies how AI stages subject-like coherence while remaining fundamentally dependent on difference and heterogeneity.

items.title: Racial and ethnic disparities in cardiac surgery and the emerging role of artificial intelligence: applications, bias, and equity challenges
items.abstract: Cardiac surgery is no stranger to innovation. The heart-lung machine enabled the first open heart surgery by John Gibbon in 1953 (1), followed by Coronary Artery Bypass Graft (CABG), pioneered by René Favaloro (2), and the first cardiac transplant by Christiaan Barnard in 1967, made more feasible in the 1970s by cyclosporine (1). More recently, minimally invasive cardiac surgery (MICS) has gained traction for its faster recovery, improved outcomes and reduced surgical trauma (3), and has been further advanced by robotics such as the da Vinci system (4). The push to integrate artificial intelligence (AI) into cardiac care is therefore unsurprising. Current efforts use machine learning to predict pre- and post-operative risks and complications (5−7), and enhanced imaging to predict complications and disease progression (8)(9). Our concern is that these advances may outpace efforts to ensure equitable surgical care. Although AI is often perceived as neutral, it may perpetuate disparities depending on how it is developed and validated. Deep learning models can predict self-reported race from chest radiographs, CT scans, and mammograms with high accuracy, even after image corruption and when human experts cannot (10). While this ability does not by itself establish biased performance or harm, it raises concern that models may exploit demographic information in clinical predictions. Evaluating subgroup performance and downstream outcomes is therefore essential to equitable AI implementation. This review examines racial and ethnic disparities in CABG, valve repair and replacement, and heart transplantation in the United States, across referral, diagnosis, intervention, and postoperative outcomes. It also considers AI’s implications for access, clinical decision-making, and risk prediction, and the risk of algorithmic bias for racial and ethnic minority populations.
