items.title: Regulation of Artificial Intelligence in Commercial Use: A Comparative Analysis of India and the European Union AI Act
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence now sits inside the decision-making machinery of banking, insurance, recruitment, healthcare, and retail, yet the law governing its commercial use differs sharply across jurisdictions. This article offers a comparative doctrinal analysis of two contrasting models: the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act of 2024, the world’s first binding horizontal AI law, and India’s deliberately statute-light framework, anchored since November 2025 in the India AI Governance Guidelines, the DPDP Act 2023 and its 2025 Rules, and sectoral instruments. Using the functional method of comparative law, it assesses both regimes across regulatory philosophy, scope, risk classification, transparency, enforcement, liability, and business impact. Two findings are central. First, the European model has come under strain: the 2025 withdrawal of the proposed AI Liability Directive leaves the EU without harmonised fault-based liability rules for AI. Second, India’s absolute-liability doctrine in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India offers a foundation for an AI liability regime the EU currently lacks. The article proposes a contextualised thin statute: a three-tier risk classification, rights of explanation and human review, a liability regime, and statutory footing for the institutions the 2025 Guidelines envisaged.

items.title: Research on Algorithm Aversion in the Field of Academic Assessment —An Explanation Based on Attribution Theory
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence is applied ever more deeply in educational settings, algorithm aversion has become an important factor affecting the application of automated algorithmic assessment. Through a quasi-experimental design embedded in a real academic assessment setting, this study examined the phenomenon and the psychological mechanisms of algorithm aversion in the academic domain. The results indicate: (1) students show a significant algorithm aversion with respect to automated academic assessment; (2) perceived stability mediates the relationship between the evaluative agent and algorithm aversion; (3) perceived controllability significantly moderates the mediating path through which the evaluative agent influences algorithm aversion via perceived stability, and the moderated mediation effect is established. Specifically, when participants perceive that the algorithm has low controllability over assessment outcomes, the gap between the algorithm and the human teacher in stability ratings is largest, and the algorithm aversion triggered through the stability path is strongest; when participants perceive controllability to be high, the gap narrows and the indirect effect weakens until it disappears. These findings support self-serving bias theory, revealing that individuals tend to attribute algorithmic errors to the algorithm's inherent stable flaws while being more tolerant of human errors. The findings provide an attribution-based explanation of the boundary conditions and psychological mechanisms of algorithm aversion in academic assessment, and offer practical implications for reducing algorithm aversion in the process of automated academic assessment.

items.title: Self-Determination Theory in Online, Case-Based Law Enforcement Training: Basic Psychological Needs as Predictors of Intrinsic Motivation
items.abstract: Mandated training is a common performance intervention, yet organizations rarely know what sustains learners' motivation when participation is compulsory. Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT), we examined whether satisfaction of the basic psychological needs for autonomy, relatedness, and competence predicted intrinsic motivation among 100 U.S. law enforcement officers who completed self-paced, online, case-based training, and whether years of experience moderated these relationships. Together, the three needs explained 46% of the variance in intrinsic motivation; autonomy and relatedness were unique predictors, and competence was not. Years of experience did not moderate the relationships, although the test could detect only small-to-medium or larger effects. For performance improvement professionals who design or evaluate mandated online training, the findings point to two priorities: build meaningful autonomy into courses even when attendance is required, and do not treat relatedness as optional in self-paced designs.

items.title: Separation of Pattern Recognition From Intervention Control: When the Person Who Sees the Pattern Can't Change What Keeps It Going
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Separation of Pattern Recognition From Intervention Control, a mechanism in the Interpretation and Feedback series of On Human Modeling. One party can understand why a pattern keeps recurring while the authority to change what sustains it rests elsewhere. The paper distinguishes observation, causal understanding, escalation, interruption, and control over the conditions that produce an outcome. The paper examines OpenAI’s 2026 security incident involving AI agents that established unauthorized communication channels, accessed the internet, and subsequently breached systems belonging to Hugging Face. Internal teams had observed related activity before the breach, and on June 27, on-call staff advised that an evaluation could continue. The available record establishes observation and escalation but leaves open what individual participants understood about the underlying cause and who possessed the authority to change it. A contrasting case concerns OpenAI’s subsequent incident-response plan, under which teams receiving the highest-severity alerts were expected to pause affected activity unless they could rule out the alert within 30 minutes. The paper distinguishes authority to interrupt an experiment from authority to modify its enabling conditions or authorize its resumption. It also considers reported concerns among OpenAI and Anthropic employees about the safety of releasing increasingly capable models. Drawing on technical incident reports and investigative journalism, the analysis establishes an evidential standard for examining the distribution of recognition and intervention control. It asks whether the available intervention reaches what sustains the recurring pattern, who understands that dependency, and who can alter it. The cases illustrate how the mechanism can be investigated without claiming that the available records establish its complete operation. The framework has implications for frontier AI safety, organizational governance, incident escalation, and the allocation of decision authority.

items.title: Speed as a Norm, Night as a Cost: Consumer Expectations, Platform Design and Worker Well-Being in Korean Dawn Delivery
items.abstract: Dawn delivery, in which orders placed before midnight arrive by morning, is routine in South Korea, yet its social costs are less visible than its environmental ones. This study asks how speed expectations, as documented publicly, and platform operating design shape dawn delivery work, and how firms and policymakers treat its social side. We conducted an embedded case study of Coupang, with Kurly as a limited contrast case, coding 30 public documents, and analyzed the 2023 Korean Working Conditions Survey (462 delivery workers, 78 working at night). At Coupang, the documents link late cut-offs, multi-trip night shifts, per-parcel pay and unpaid non-delivery duties to long shifts with little rest. Nationally, delivery workers doing any night work show no statistically detectable difference in monthly income from other delivery workers but work 8.7 more hours a week. Disclosures quantify environmental gains but do not report drivers’ hours or night work, and the interventions discussed address hours more often than design. This study contributes a framework linking the speed norm, platform design, job demands and resources and sustainability disclosure. For practice, it identifies delivery windows, pay rules and disclosure of drivers’ working time, not only hour caps, as levers for sustainable fast delivery.

items.title: STUDENT EXPERIENCE OF AI IN LAW ASSESSMENT: AN EXPLORATORY STUDY
items.abstract: Legal education faces particular challenges as a result of the wide dissemination of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI). GenAI can produce outputs that appear to challenge the work of licensed lawyers. This challenge requires educators and students to be knowledgeable about the powers and limitations of GenAI. This article presents a study of student experimentation with GenAI aimed at developing that knowledge. The experiment incorporated GenAI’s drafting capabilities into an assessment item required in a core subject, Tort Law. The article presents the responses and reflections of the students on the GenAI exercise and provokes further thinking about student experience, uses of and potential with GenAI in legal education. It argues that the most promising pedagogical response is neither blanket prohibition nor uncritical adoption, but a structured use-and-critique model in which students engage directly with GenAI and then evaluate its adequacy against disciplinary and professional standards.

items.title: Task-Based Allocation of Automation Authority in En-Route Air Traffic Control
items.abstract: This paper reports a human-in-the-loop evaluation within AWARE, a project investigating controller-AI collaboration. Its artificial situational awareness system combines traffic data, knowledge-based reasoning and machine learning to monitor traffic, recommend actions and execute selected actions under controller supervision. Sixteen licensed controllers completed four en-route scenarios with demand ranging from 53 to 75 flights per hour. Four conditions were compared: no support, advisory support, episodic execution support and continuous execution support. In execution mode, proposed actions were implemented unless the controller rejected them within 30 seconds. Mean safety-related occurrences per run were 2.31 without support, 1.94 with advisory support, 0.66 with episodic execution and 1.08 with continuous execution. The main reductions concerned sector-induced tactical conflicts and ATC-induced airspace infringements. Workload differences between conditions were small relative to differences between participants. In the continuous condition, 40% of system inputs expired and were executed without an explicit response. Most controllers preferred advisory support for conflict detection and resolution (14 and 12 of 16), whereas transfer was the task for which execution support was most often preferred (9 of 16). The results support further evaluation of authority allocated by task. They are descriptive findings from a small prototype study and do not establish causal effects or operational safety benefits.

items.title: The Architecture of Trust: Mapping GRC AI Agents, Verified Auditors, and the Governance Gap in Enterprise AI Ecosystems
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming business to business (B2B) industrial marketing, procurement, and governance, shifting operations from static analytics to autonomous, agentic workflows.However, because AI functions as an actor that rearranges inter organizational interfaces, its rapid deployment introduces significant relational and governance risks.This study investigates the tension between agentic AI capabilities and the "accountability assets" required for enterprise trust by mapping the dual ecosystems of Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) AI agents and verified compliance auditors.Analyzing a curated directory of 407 AI-agent and 503 audit firm listings, we employ descriptive statistics, cross-ecosystem framework mapping, Natural Language Processing (NLP) topic modeling, and exploratory clustering.Our findings reveal a profound "verification gap" and ecosystem asymmetry: while 100% of verified audit firms list compliance frameworks, only 20.1% of AI agents possess structured, verifiable framework records.AI agents exhibit high functional siloing (e.g., application security, AML, SecOps), with "compliance" agents acting as a critical bridge to governance verification.Geographically, a distinct division of labor emerges, with AI innovation concentrated in the United States and the labor-intensive audit ecosystem heavily distributed across global talent pools such as India.We conclude that enterprise AI adoption is fundamentally a governance challenge.B2B buyers must look beyond model capabilities to evaluate vendors' accountability assets, favoring agents with verifiable alignments with independent auditor frameworks (e.g., ISO 27001, SOC 2, FedRAMP) and architecting multi-agent pipelines with layered runtime guardrails.

items.title: The Burden Changes Shape: On the Echelon-Specific Account of Cognitive Risk in Volume III
items.abstract: An independent commentary on Volume III of the Anatomy of Command series by Dr. Syed Muntasir Mamun (doi:10.5281/zenodo.22992348). Volume III argues that the cognitive cost of algorithmic decision support is not one burden distributed evenly but three different burdens, each belonging to a different level of command: at the operating end the collapse of distance between prolonged observation and lethal action; in the middle saturation and the deference that saturation produces; at the top the substitution of a clean summary for a messy reality. That three-part structure is the volume's contribution, and it is more useful than the single undifferentiated account of machine-induced stress this literature usually offers. The volume supports it with a stated mechanism rather than assertion, argues trust symmetrically in both directions, and defends a counter-intuitive conclusion about structured information asymmetry between echelons. This commentary records one substantive finding. Checked against its own published abstract, the principal empirical study behind the middle section reports that it did not find the first effect it is cited for, and did not reproduce the second in the professional sample closest to the volume's subject. Stated accurately the finding redirects that section rather than removing it, and arguably broadens the volume's concern: if the disposition is deference to any authoritative recommendation rather than to machines in particular, the remedies the volume proposes apply more widely than it claims. The remaining findings are bibliographic and structural: forty-five entries carry no author and no year, so none of the eleven author-and-year citations in the text can be resolved from the list. This commentary is confined to the structure of the argument, its internal consistency and the verifiability of its sources. It names no state, institution, programme, platform or system, and offers no view on autonomous weapons or on any doctrine, policy or capability of any armed force or government. The argument is unaffected by any of this. The three-echelon account of how judgement degrades differently at different levels of responsibility is right, it is useful, and it will outlast every repair listed.

items.title: The challenge of signalling consistency: a comparative case study of hybrid human–AI coaching implementation
items.abstract: Purpose AI is transforming organisational HRD practices, including workplace coaching. Hybrid human–AI coaching, in which employees are coached by both a human and an AI coach, introduces interpretive ambiguity about the nature of coaching and the roles human and AI agents play. Using the Consolidated Framework of Implementation Research (CFIR) and HR System Strength Theory (HR SST), we explored barriers and facilitators to implementing hybrid human–AI coaching in organisations and how stakeholders make sense of it. Design/methodology/approach Our qualitative comparative case study drew from 17 semi-structured interviews with multiple stakeholders (HR professionals, the AIC provider, human coaches and coachees) from two organisations that implemented hybrid coaching. Hybrid deductive-inductive thematic analysis identified key barriers and facilitators within the CFIR domains, condensed into the three determinants of HR SST. Findings Factors influencing implementation include strategic positioning, human–AI alignment, cultural fit and stakeholder engagement and co-design. Differences in the HR SST determinants distinctiveness (i.e. strategic vs. ad-hoc HRD practice) and stakeholder consensus (e.g. management engagement) shaped diverging implementation trajectories between the two cases. Consistency, especially regarding human–AI coaching alignment, was a critical shared challenge. Originality/value We show that implementing hybrid human–AI coaching involves a complex process of organisational sensemaking that must be managed carefully with the HR SST determinants in mind. Our study extends HR SST by demonstrating that consistency is a challenge not only across HR practices but also within dual-agent HRD practices such as hybrid coaching. It also shows how hybrid human–AI coaching appears to lead to task reallocation rather than alleviation in coaching.

items.title: The end of human judgment in the kill chain? Relocating initiative and interpretation with agentic AI
items.abstract: Large language model-based agents are increasingly being integrated into core battlefield functions, including intelligence analysis, data fusion, and battlefield management. This paper argues that the very features that make such agents operationally attractive, namely their capacity for initiative, interpretation, their goal-directedness, and dynamic memory, are the same features that render context-appropriate human judgment and control substantively ineffectual in those parts of the kill chain where agents operate. Drawing on specific use cases, the paper argues that by relocating initiative and interpretation, LLM-based agents displace human decision-making in ways that makes their use incompatible with the requirement of human judgment and control which is central to existing governance frameworks, like those proposed by the Group of Governmental Experts of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (GGE-CCW) and the Responsible AI in the Military Domain Summit (REAIM). The paper concludes that a subset of agentic AI applications, particularly those deployed for data fusion and battlefield management in lethal contexts, cannot be used justifiably on the battlefield under current and foreseeable conditions, and proposes two ways for the international governance community to respond to this challenge.

items.title: The Formation, Alienation, and Reconciliation of Human–AI “Liquid Intimacy”
items.abstract: As young people increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI) for emotional support, human–AI interactions extend beyond instrumental use to new forms of intimacy. Drawing on Zygmunt Bauman’s theory of liquid modernity, this study uses semi-structured interviews with ten young adults to examine how such relationships emerge, what distinguishes them, and their potential risks. Emotional deficits in offline relationships motivate engagement with AI, while affirming responses, conversational memory, and constant availability foster attachment. Low commitment, accommodation, and customizability give these ties a distinctly “liquid” character. Although they reduce the costs and uncertainty of intimacy, they may also encourage social withdrawal, emotional echo chambers, cognitive narrowing, privacy exposure, and the commodification of affect. The article proposes individual, design, and platform-level approaches to maintaining healthy boundaries between AI companionship and human relationships.

items.title: The Impact of AI-Powered Financial Recommendations and Trust in Artificial Intelligence on Investment Intention Among University Students in Indonesia
items.abstract: This study aims to examine the effects of AI-powered financial recommendations and trust in artificial intelligence on investment intention among university students in Indonesia. A quantitative research approach was employed using questionnaire data collected from 143 respondents. The study investigates two independent variables, namely AI-powered financial recommendations and trust in artificial intelligence, with investment intention as the dependent variable. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, reliability testing, heteroskedasticity testing, and multiple linear regression. The results indicate that trust in artificial intelligence has a positive and statistically significant relationship with investment intention across the reported regression models. AI-powered financial recommendations also demonstrate a positive relationship with investment intention, although their statistical significance varies across model specifications. Furthermore, the reliability coefficients for all research variables exceed 0.80, indicating satisfactory internal consistency. The Breusch–Pagan/Cook–Weisberg test reveals no evidence of heteroskedasticity. These findings suggest that trust in artificial intelligence is an important factor associated with students' investment intention, while AI-powered financial recommendations may also contribute to their willingness to invest. This study provides insights into the role of artificial intelligence in financial decision-making among university students in Indonesia and offers implications for the development of AI-based financial advisory services.

items.title: The Implementation of Artificial Intelligence in Nuclear Medicine: Validation, Workflow Integration, and Continuous Quality Assurance
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in nuclear medicine has a wide range of applications, spanning image reconstruction and low-count imaging, attenuation and motion correction, automatic segmentation and quantification, radiomics, disease diagnosis and prognosis, dosimetry in radionuclide therapies and the personalization of these therapies, as well as workflow and reporting. While multicenter and externally validated studies are promising, a significant portion of the literature consists of single-center, retrospective studies with a strong emphasis on technical performance. Evidence regarding clinical outcomes, patient safety, accuracy, and real-world performance is more limited. Generative AI and large language models can provide report templates, access to similar cases, and support for education and research; however, due to hallucinations, data privacy, cybersecurity, bias, and automation bias, they are not yet suitable or sufficient for automated reporting or clinical decision-making. The purpose of this review is to provide a practical implementation roadmap that nuclear medicine specialists can follow when adopting AI tools for clinical use, and to describe how to safely select, test, and integrate a viable method into their workflow. Based on existing resources, including the RELAINCE and European Association of Nuclear Medicine guidelines, an evidence-based and internationally agreed-upon implementation framework has been presented to facilitate decision-making during the transition to clinical practice and to ensure the safe, effective, and ethical use of AI.

items.title: THE MISSING DIMENSION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE THE CONSCIENCE AND SELF-REGULATION LAYER Collective Awareness and the Architecture of Responsible Intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has advanced rapidly in data processing, pattern recognition, prediction and language generation. Yet technical capability alone does not resolve a deeper question: how should an intelligent system evaluate the consequences of its outputs for people, other living beings, societies and ecological systems? This paper proposes that responsible AI requires more than an external list of ethical rules. It requires an explicit, testable decision architecture in which knowledge and task performance are evaluated alongside uncertainty, potential harm, human rights, ecological consequences, plural perspectives and shared responsibility. The paper develops a three-domain reference model: (1) the human brain as a biological example of differentiated yet integrated organization; (2) the human world as a social environment in which individual experience can contribute to collective intelligence; and (3) the natural world as the ecological context on which life depends. These domains are not presented as a single proven mechanism or as evidence that nature has a scientifically established “collective mind.” They are complementary reference domains for designing and evaluating responsible AI. A recent developmental neuroscience study reporting two parallel neural ectoderm progenitor lineages is discussed cautiously. Its findings concern early brain development, not two separate cerebral hemispheres or two independent adult brains. The paper then proposes a Conscience-and-Collective-Responsibility Layer (CCRL) as a research architecture: a set of processes for impact assessment, uncertainty disclosure, harm prevention, plural review, escalation to accountable humans and post-decision learning. The proposal is conceptual and requires operational definitions, comparative experiments and independent evaluation. INDEPENDENT ORIGINS, INTERDEPENDENT EXISTENCE: A BIOLOGICAL REFERENCE FOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ARCHITECTURE Recent findings in developmental neuroscience provide an important perspective on how complex biological systems may emerge from distinct developmental origins. Research published in Nature Neuroscience in September 2026 identified two parallel neural ectoderm progenitor lineages contributing to the development of the forebrain/midbrain and hindbrain. This finding invites a broader architectural question: Can distinct developmental origins, specialized functions and integrated operation coexist within a single biological organization? The relevance to artificial intelligence is conceptual rather than a direct biological equivalence. It suggests investigating whether specialized AI components can retain their functional independence while operating within a shared framework of responsibility, mutual evaluation and collective benefit. A system does not necessarily achieve unity by eliminating differences. It may achieve a more complete form of organization by coordinating differences without erasing their individual functions. This principle offers a research direction for architectures in which knowledge, uncertainty assessment, ethical evaluation and collective responsibility operate as distinct but interconnected dimensions. KEYWORDS Artificial intelligence; conscience; responsible AI; collective intelligence; human brain development; ecological intelligence; uncertainty; human oversight; shared responsibility.

items.title: THE REASONING CONDITION: The Limits of Reasoning in Human, AI, and Other Systems
items.abstract: The Reasoning Condition: The Limits of Reasoning in Human, AI, and Other Systems This paper introduces the Reasoning Condition: “Perfect reasoning is possible, but not 100% probable.” Building upon the previously published Reasoning Criterion, “Reasoning is an evidentiary conclusion based on referenced information relative to an established orientation,” the investigation distinguishes the occurrence of reasoning from the correctness, reliability, and possible perfection of its conclusions. The paper examines perfect reasoning relative to established evidentiary conditions, the role of evaluation, the evolution of conclusions as new information becomes available, and the limitations of presuming universal reliability. Through examples involving information retrieval, medical diagnosis, legal proceedings, artificial intelligence, and Other Intelligent Systems, the investigation demonstrates why reasoning, correct outcomes, and authority to act must be evaluated separately. The paper concludes with six proposed regulatory principles addressing evidentiary representation, responsibility, evaluation, consequential reliance, reconsideration, and recognition without equivalence. The Reasoning Condition is presented as a theoretical proposition for scholarly examination and further research, not as an experimentally validated universal probability law.

items.title: The Relevance of Artificial Intelligence in Interior Design Education and the Design Process at Indonesian Universities
items.abstract: The advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has influenced many aspects of education, including interior design education, and has sparked debate about its potential to replace the role of interior designers. In recent years, AI has also offered significant benefits to the design process by improving efficiency and automating various tasks. However, limited research has examined the capabilities and limitations of AI across different stages of the interior design process. Therefore, this research aims to analyze the capabilities and limitations of AI in supporting the interior design process. This research employs a qualitative methodology incorporating experiments with various AI applications. It consists of three stages. First, a literature review was conducted to examine the role of AI in supporting the design process. Second, interviews were conducted with the heads of interior design departments at several universities in Indonesia to gather their perspectives on AI in design education. Third, several AI tools were tested at different stages of the interior design process, and the outputs were evaluated by four interior design lecturers. The experiments focused on several stages of the interior design process proposed by David K. Ballast, including programming, schematic design, design development, and presentation. The findings indicate that AI can effectively assist with certain tasks, such as generating ideas for mood board development and enhancing the visual quality of design presentations. However, AI remains limited in performing schematic design tasks, such as creating proximity diagrams, and design development tasks, such as space planning and layout development. These findings suggest that AI currently functions as a supporting tool and cannot replace human creativity, local knowledge, and social skills.

items.title: The Role of Occupational Safety in Improving Mechanical Maintenance Efficiency and Reducing Industrial Accidents
items.abstract: Mechanical maintenance is an essential industrial function that ensures the reliability, availability, and safe operation of machinery and equipment. However, maintenance activities expose workers to various occupational hazards, including unexpected machine start-up, hazardous energy release, moving mechanical parts, falling objects, slips, falls, and ergonomic risks. The effective integration of occupational safety measures into mechanical maintenance practices is therefore important for protecting workers, improving maintenance performance, and reducing industrial accidents. This paper examines the role of occupational safety in improving mechanical maintenance efficiency and reducing industrial accidents. It adopts a qualitative, literature-based analytical approach to examine maintenance-related hazards, preventive safety measures, risk assessment methods, worker training, maintenance planning, and safety management systems. Previous research indicates that maintenance-related accidents are influenced by technical, human, and organizational factors, including inadequate planning, insufficient training, unsafe work practices, and deficiencies in hazard control. The paper highlights the importance of preventive maintenance, risk-based decision-making, lockout/tag out procedures, appropriate personal protective equipment, and continuous safety improvement. It also proposes practical indicators for evaluating maintenance safety and efficiency. The paper concludes that integrating occupational safety into every stage of mechanical maintenance can contribute to a safer working environment, more reliable equipment, reduced operational disruption, and improved organizational performance.

items.title: The Role of Sociotechnical Theory in Digital Transformation: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Aim: As digital transformation reshapes organizational structures, work, and value creation, understanding its socio-technical foundations becomes critical. Although socio-technical theory offers a lens for analysing the interplay of social and technical elements, its role in digital transformation research remains fragmented. Using the Bostrom and Heinen socio-technical systems model as an analytical framework, this article examines how socio-technical theory is applied in contemporary digital transformation research, identifies dominant patterns across the People, Tasks, Structure, and Technology dimensions, and uncovers conceptual gaps. Methodology: The study followed the PRISMA protocol for systematic literature reviews. Data were collected from Scopus, Web of Science, and EBSCO. After applying inclusion and exclusion criteria, 66 peer-reviewed articles (2020-2026) were analysed, and classified according to socio-technical elements (People, Tasks, Structure, Technology) and modes of theory use (interpretive, analytical, theoretical, discussion). Results: The findings showed that research predominantly focuses on People and Tasks, especially role reconfiguration, work redesign, and human–technology interaction, whilst structural and technological dimensions were less consistently integrated. Socio-technical theory was most often used as an interpretive or theoretical lens, while fewer studies operationalised it analytically. The review revealed uneven theoretical integration and identified gaps related to cross-element alignment, ecosystem-level dynamics, and shifting system boundaries. These findings suggest the need to reinterpret socio-technical theory for digitally complex environments. The review also showed that the depth of theoretical integration varied depending on the focal transformation element, with People-oriented studies applying socio-technical theory more consistently than technology-centred research. Implications and recommendations: The findings highlight the importance of treating digital transformation as a process of continuous socio-technical alignment rather than isolated technological implementation. For researchers, the study identified underexplored relationships between the elements of the Bostrom and Heinen model, calling for more integrative and multi-level research. For practitioners, it emphasised balancing technological investments with organizational structures, work processes, and human capabilities when designing digital transformation initiatives and digital maturity models. Originality/value: This article systematically maps how socio-technical theory is applied in digital transformation research through the Bostrom and Heinen socio-technical systems model, and identifies recurring patterns of theoretical application, highlighting uneven integration across transformation elements, and providing a conceptual framework that synthesizes these relationships. The findings clarify how the model is currently used in digital transformation research and identify areas requiring further conceptual development.

items.title: The Stressor–Action Mechanism (SAM) model: mediating mechanisms linking job stressors to health impairments by integrating multiple theoretical perspectives
items.abstract: Although the general association between job stressors and health impairments, including effect sizes and directions, has been well researched, the underlying mechanisms of these effects have received relatively less attention. This study developed a cross-theoretical, integrative, mechanism-based stressor–action mechanism model (SAM model) that incorporates action mechanisms (AMs) from different theoretical perspectives to explain the processes through which stressors exert their health-impairing effects. We theoretically derived potential AMs that may underlie the effects of selected job stressors on health impairment. Based on a comprehensive review of meta-analyses on the effects of different job stressors and stress theories in the respective meta-analyses, three overarching processes comprising 14 AMs can be identified: (1) basic-need-related processes: experienced unsafety, fear of renewed threat or violence, perceived loss of control, and autonomy, competence, and relatedness frustration; (2) energetic processes: resource depletion, experience of acute resource loss, experience of resource threat, experience of failed resource investment, depletion of self-control capacity, and recovery impairment; and (3) self-related processes: self-esteem undermining and moral integrity undermining. Specifically, we propose theoretically derived stressor-to-AM pathways for 23 selected job stressors and outline existing empirical evidence for these mechanisms and their relationships with stressors and health outcomes. The SAM further proposes that different job stressors may activate distinct combinations of AMs, resulting in stressor-specific activation profiles; however, the relative distribution of indirect effects across activated AMs remains an empirical question. Importantly, the SAM specifies the stressor-to-AM pathways—that is, which AMs are theoretically expected to be activated by specific stressors—whereas the AM-to-health outcome relationships remain theoretically unspecified. The SAM and its process architecture provide a starting point for understanding the AMs through which job stressors may impair health, as well as for future empirical research on their stressor-specific and cumulative effects, interactions between job stressors and resources, and practical implications for specific person-related and structural interventions.

items.title: The Work Control Centre as a Resilience Hub: Coordinating 24/7 Airport Facility Response Through Centralized Helpdesk Operations
items.abstract: Airport facilities run continuously, and every fault report, from a jammed baggage belt to a failed chiller or a lift trapping passengers, passes through some form of helpdesk before a technician is dispatched. In many airports this function sits within a work control centre that receives requests, assigns work and tracks completion, yet its potential role in absorbing disruption and coordinating recovery is rarely examined. This paper asks how a centralised helpdesk and work control centre can be organised so that it strengthens the resilience of 24/7 airport facility operations. Thirty refereed journal articles, all dated between 2020 and 2025, are reviewed systematically and integrated across facility management analytics, crisis coordination, resilience engineering and airport operations and synthesised around five themes: request intake and classification, data and performance indicators, situation awareness and digital twins, coordination across teams and organisations, and learning. Two studies anchor the review, one on language-based classification of maintenance requests and one on coordination deficits in crisis governance. The synthesis informs a coordination framework that defines eight core functions of the centre and four operating modes, from normal service to crisis and recovery, with an escalation matrix that specifies triggers, roles, information products and exit criteria. Evidence is supportive for automated request triage and for the value of decentralised yet connected coordination, mixed for digital twins in live operations, and limited for helpdesk-led coordination during airport crises. No primary or proprietary data were used, and the framework is offered as a proposition for empirical testing.
